caption:
🏆 Congratulations, Kristina G. Douglass! The archaeologist and Associate Professor of Climate at @ColumbiaClimate has been named a 2025 MacArthur Fellow. 

The MacArthur Foundation “genius grant” recognizes exceptional creativity and dedication, celebrating creative potential through a no-strings-attached $800,000 fellowship.

Douglass investigates how human societies and environments have co-evolved and adapted to climate variability over time. Her research, based in southwest Madagascar, uses lessons from the past to understand how to adapt to climate change, working in close, longstanding collaborations with local and Indigenous communities.

Read more about Douglass and her work via Columbia Climate School’s State of the Planet at the link in our bio.

📷 John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation 

#ColumbiaUniversity #MacFellow @OBTLab

caption:
🌳 College Walk will look a little different when you return to Morningside campus for the fall semester! 

Our Grounds team worked with leading arborists to develop a new look that honors the historic design of College Walk while looking toward the future. 

Unfortunately, several of the older trees along the path were in declining health and presented a safety risk, and therefore needed to be removed. The revamped design will highlight the flowering Kwanzan cherry blossom trees that have lived on College Walk for decades. Linden trees will remain at either end of the Walk, and seasonal plantings will bloom near the trees. This new arrangement will open up sightlines to better take in Morningside’s grand architecture. 

Another benefit of these changes: benches will be added around the perimeter of College Walk, adding plenty of additional seating and creating new spots to gather with friends. 

We’ll see you soon on College Walk!

📷 Eileen Barroso #ColumbiaUniversity

We’re seeing a lot of comments asking why the linden trees being removed couldn’t simply be replaced. The professional arborists who evaluated the site identified that the existing linden trees were struggling due to inadequate root space, which compromised their structural integrity and long-term viability. Additionally, the cherry trees require full sunlight exposure to thrive, but their growth was being significantly stunted by the shade cast by the larger linden canopy.
